title: Thám hiểm và nhu cầu Trái Đất · Two-part question
prompt: There is growing debate about funding human missions to other planets while urgent social needs remain unmet. Why might people support this approach, and what should decision-makers consider before adopting it?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Đề có hai câu hỏi: vì sao có người ủng hộ và phải cân nhắc điều gì trước khi áp dụng. Thân một giải thích động cơ, thân hai kiểm tra chi phí và điều kiện khả thi. Không coi khả năng có công nghệ phụ là lợi ích chắc chắn hoặc đủ để bỏ nhu cầu cấp bách. Cần so nhiệm vụ có người với nghiên cứu rẻ hơn hoặc không người đạt mục tiêu tương tự. Minh bạch chi phí và giữ dịch vụ thiết yếu đặt giới hạn phân bổ. Bài phải giải thích vì sao sứ mệnh cụ thể đáng đầu tư ở thời điểm này, không bảo vệ mọi dự án mang nhãn khám phá.
outline.content: Support for human planetary missions reflects hopes of scientific discovery and engineering capabilities that could also improve technologies used on Earth. Before funding them, governments should compare their additional scientific value with robotic alternatives and the essential services forgone, rather than regard possible technological spillovers as sufficient justification.

paragraphs: Support for human planetary missions reflects hopes of scientific discovery and engineering capabilities that could also improve technologies used on Earth. Before funding them, governments should compare their additional scientific value with robotic alternatives and the essential services forgone, rather than regard possible technological spillovers as sufficient justification.

Space missions can develop scientific capabilities with benefits beyond a single destination. Demanding engineering problems encourage collaboration and produce expertise that can be applied elsewhere. Work on reliable life-support systems could inform resource-efficient technologies. The possible benefit is accumulated technical competence, which needs a plausible route into wider use rather than a claim that every ambitious mission produces transformative inventions. Life-support research may produce useful expertise, but similar gains might be achievable through less costly research without sending people to another planet.

Prestige projects can absorb resources without offering a credible answer to immediate deprivation. Human missions require expensive safety and life-support systems, so their additional cost needs a stronger justification than a general enthusiasm for scientific progress. If promised applications remain speculative, scarce public resources may be diverted from urgent services with more immediate and credible benefits. Mission budgets should be transparent and should not displace essential public services. Independent comparison with robotic missions and terrestrial research can test additional value, while protected service budgets keep uncertain future benefits from automatically overriding urgent needs. A mission should justify its additional scientific value and opportunity cost, with essential services protected rather than speculative spillovers treated as guaranteed compensation for present deprivation.

Thus, scientific ambition explains public support, but adoption requires a credible comparison of additional benefits, mission costs and urgent terrestrial needs; possible discovery alone does not resolve the spending decision.

paragraphs.quote: Prestige projects can absorb resources without offering a credible answer to immediate deprivation. Human missions require expensive safety and life-support systems, so their additional cost needs a stronger justification than a general enthusiasm for scientific progress. If promised applications remain speculative, scarce public resources may be diverted from urgent services with more immediate and credible benefits. Mission budgets should be transparent and should not displace essential public services. Independent comparison with robotic missions and terrestrial research can test additional value, while protected service budgets keep uncertain future benefits from automatically overriding urgent needs. A mission should justify its additional scientific value and opportunity cost, with essential services protected rather than speculative spillovers treated as guaranteed compensation for present deprivation.
